sections.title: Qur'anic Letter Distribution and Authenticity
sections.summary: Yusuf Amin Wali presents a mathematical analysis of letter distribution in the Qur'an, specifically examining the letter Qaf in suras Al-Shura and Qaf. The author corrects a previous publication, clarifying that while these two Qaf-initialed suras each contain 57 Qafs totaling 114 (matching the number of Qur'anic suras), sura Ibrahim contains 57 Qafs only when initials are excluded. This mathematical precision is argued as evidence of divine authorship.

sections.title: The Gospel of Barnabas: Authenticity and Reliability
sections.summary: S. Shahid Mufassir presents a comprehensive critical analysis of the Gospel of Barnabas, arguing that the Italian manuscript discovered by Pope Sixtus V cannot be an authentic first-century Christian text. The author identifies linguistic evidence (defective Hebrew, reliance on the Latin Vulgate), historical anachronisms (Papal Jubilee dating to 1300-1350 CE), and theological inconsistencies that contradict both Islamic and Christian orthodoxy. Mufassir distinguishes this fabrication from the fragmentary Greek Gospel of Barnabas mentioned by Christian scholars and discusses the occurrence of PERIKLYTOS (understood as Muhammad) in the Gospel of John.

sections.title: Islamic Sacred History and Jerusalem
sections.summary: Ahmad Taha from Al-Azhar University presents Jerusalem's significance within Islamic tradition and doctrine. He establishes that Jerusalem holds unique status as a holy city for Islam, Christianity, and Judaism. The author details the Prophet Muhammad's nocturnal journey (Isra') from Jerusalem to Heaven and the role of Jerusalem as the first Qibla (prayer direction) for Muslims. Taha documents the Dome of the Rock's Islamic architectural significance, the 1099 Crusader conquest, and Saladin's 1187 recapture. He emphasizes thirteen centuries of Muslim custodianship of sacred Christian and Jewish sites, citing General Allenby's 1917 recognition of this stewardship.

sections.title: Hadith Falsification: Origins and Historical Development
sections.summary: Muhammad 'Ajjaj Al-Khatib from the University of Damascus presents a comprehensive historical analysis of how the Hadith (Prophet's traditions) were subject to falsification and fabrication. Al-Khatib establishes that while the Qur'an received divine protection, the Hadith literature faced deliberate distortion, misinterpretation, and fabrication by various groups. The author traces the historical development of false hadith creation, documenting how political factions, theological schools, and fabricators introduced spurious traditions into Islamic jurisprudence. The work emphasizes the methodological challenges in separating authentic from inauthentic hadiths and the devastating impact of such falsifications on Islamic practice and belief.

sections.title: Hadith Verification Methods and Scholarly Criteria
sections.summary: Continuing Al-Khatib's analysis, this section focuses on the sophisticated methodologies developed by Islamic scholars to authenticate hadith collections. Al-Khatib discusses specific examples of false hadiths, their creators' motivations, and how rigorous hadith science (ilm al-hadith) established criteria for authenticity. The work demonstrates how Islamic scholarship developed robust systems for textual preservation and reliability despite political and theological pressures to manipulate traditions.
